newsitem.title: USA: George Burns memorabilia brings high prices.
newsitem.headline: George Burns memorabilia brings high prices.

text.p: Memorabilia from the estate of late comedian, actor and singer George Burns was put up for bids on Thursday, and fetched prices that surprised even the venerable Sotheby's auction house, which organised the sale.
The 226-item auction, the proceeds of which were to go to three of Burns' favourite charities, took in a total of $365,792, compared to Sotheby's expectations of $300,000.
A crowd of more than 200 people, which included as many fans as memorabilia dealers, flocked to Sotheby's auction room in Beverly Hills to snap up some of the star's personal items.

A pair of his signature round glasses went for $11,000, compared to Sotheby's projected $1,500, sending an audible gasp around the room, and a pair of gold and diamond cuff links, with initials "GB-100" went for $11,000, far above the expected price of $400 to $600.
Burns, who died in March at the age of 100, willed the proceeds of the sale to the Cedars-Sinai Medical Centre in Los Angeles, the United Jewish Fund and the Motion Picture and Television Fund.

Burns' gray and black velvet smoking jacket and his red velvet slippers were snapped up for $3,500 compared to the $500 to $700 Sotheby's had thought they would fetch, while his walking cane strolled away for $1,100, much more than the Sotheby's original price-tag of $100 to $150.

Other surprises included the eye glasses of his late wife and comedic partner, Gracie Allen -- which Burns kept by his bedside after her death in 1964 -- fetched $1,600 and which Sotheby's had shortsightedly put a $400-$600 price tag on.

Burns also left for posterity 90 of his trademark cigars, which were bought for $1,000 -- a bargain at $11.11 apiece. But as any cigar smoker knows, a humidor is necessary to keep them in perfect shape, and the big ticket item at the auction was a large wooden humidor with a plaque reading, "Presented to George Burns, Cigar Smoker of the Year 1952" by the Cigar Institute of America. It sucked in $57,500.
The cigar buyer will have to look for another device to keep Burns' cigars fresh, however. He was out of luck with the humidor, which went to a local realtor.
